title: The Bird That Flies Backward
blurb: The smallest bird on Earth hovers on a figure-eight wingbeat, drinks with a tongue that snaps shut, and shuts its own body down every night.

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Flies Backward
blocks.text: A hummingbird is small enough to sit in your hand. It weighs about as much as two paper clips. Its wings beat so fast that they blur. The wings hum, and that is where the name comes from. A hummingbird holds still in the air while it drinks. Its tongue flicks in and out many times a second. It drinks nectar, the sweet juice inside a flower. It also eats tiny bugs. A hummingbird can fly up, down, sideways, and backward. Most birds cannot fly backward at all. At night it goes into a deep sleep and gets very cold and still. In the morning it warms up and flies away.

3.title: The Bird That Flies Backward
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: Wings sweep in a figure eight, not up and down
About 50 wingbeats a second
Its heart can beat over 1,000 times a minute
It visits hundreds of flowers a day

blocks.prompt: How to Stand Still in the Air
blocks.text: Watch a hummingbird and you will notice something odd. It does not land on the flower. It hangs in the air in front of it, perfectly still, as if someone hung it from a string. Almost no other bird can do that. A hummingbird's wings do not flap up and down the way a robin's do. They sweep forward and back in a fast figure eight, and they lift the bird on both halves of the stroke. That is the trick. It is also why a hummingbird can fly backward, which no other bird can keep up for long. All that motion costs a lot. A hummingbird's wings beat about fifty times every second. Its heart can beat more than a thousand times a minute. To pay for it, the bird drinks nectar from hundreds of flowers a day and snaps up small insects for protein. At night, when the flowers close, it cannot afford to keep burning fuel. So it powers down. Its body cools, its heart slows to a crawl, and it sits on a twig like a cold pebble until the sun comes back.

answers: it sweeps forward and back in a figure eight; a robin flaps up and down
about fifty times a second
for protein, because nectar alone is not enough
(inference: the flowers close, so it cannot get more fuel and must save what it has)

4.title: The Bird That Flies Backward
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A ruby-throated hummingbird weighs about 3 grams
Hovering burns fuel faster than almost any animal activity
The tongue flicks about 15 times a second
Torpor: it lets its body go cold overnight
Its heart drops from over 1,000 beats a minute to about 50

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Runs on Fumes
blocks.text: A ruby-throated hummingbird weighs about three grams. That is roughly a penny and a paper clip together. Almost nothing about the bird makes sense until you understand what it costs to hover. Hovering is not resting. A hummingbird holds its place in the air by sweeping its wings forward and back in a flattened figure eight, about fifty times a second, and unlike most birds it gains lift on the backstroke as well as the forward stroke. That is why it can hang motionless in front of a flower, and why it can fly backward, sideways, and briefly upside down. It is also brutally expensive. Gram for gram, a hovering hummingbird burns energy faster than almost any other animal on Earth. The bird pays that bill with sugar. It visits hundreds of flowers a day and drinks nectar, which is close to pure fuel. Its tongue is forked at the tip and flicks in and out about fifteen times a second, trapping nectar and pulling it back. Sugar alone cannot build a body, so the hummingbird also hunts gnats, aphids, and spiders for protein. The real problem is night. Flowers close, hunting stops, and a bird this small cannot store enough fuel to burn through the dark at full power. So it does something extraordinary. It enters torpor. Its body temperature falls, its breathing turns shallow, and its heart drops from over a thousand beats a minute to around fifty. The bird hangs on a twig looking dead. At dawn it shivers itself back up to speed in a few minutes and starts again.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: Explain in your own words why hovering is so expensive for a hummingbird.
The passage says nectar is close to pure fuel. What does that mean, and why does the bird still need insects?

The author writes that the bird hangs on a twig looking dead. Why do you think a hummingbird can risk being that helpless all night?
answers: (it must beat its wings about 50 times a second to stay in one place, which burns energy faster than almost any animal activity)
nectar is almost all sugar, so it is energy but not building material; insects give protein
letting the body go cold and slow overnight; it stops the bird burning fuel it cannot replace in the dark
(inference: the alternative is running out of fuel before morning, so the risk is worth it)

5.title: The Bird That Flies Backward
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The forked tongue licks 15 to 20 times a second
Capillary action was the textbook answer for 200 years
High-speed film overturned it in 2011
Ruby-throated hummingbirds cross the Gulf of Mexico nonstop
They nearly double their weight in fat before the crossing

blocks.prompt: The Tongue That Fooled Science
blocks.text: For nearly two hundred years, biologists thought they understood how a hummingbird drinks. Look at the tongue and the answer seems obvious. It is long, thin, and split down the middle into two grooved halves, like a pair of tiny straws. Narrow tubes pull liquid upward on their own through capillary action, the same quiet force that draws water into a paper towel. Case closed. Textbooks printed it for generations. The trouble was that nobody had actually watched it happen. Capillary action is slow, and it gets slower as the liquid gets thicker. Nectar is syrup. The math never quite worked, because the tongue should not have been able to keep up with a bird that licks fifteen to twenty times a second. In 2011 a researcher named Alejandro Rico-Guevara aimed a high-speed camera through the clear wall of a feeder, filmed the tongue itself, and slowed the footage down. What he saw was not a straw. As the tongue enters the nectar, the two grooved halves spring apart and unfurl, their fringed edges spreading open. As the tongue is drawn back out, the surface of the liquid pinches the halves shut, and they close around a trapped mouthful and carry it in. The tongue is not a tube. It is a trap that reloads itself, powered by the very nectar it is catching, and it costs the bird almost nothing. This matters more than a footnote in a textbook. A hovering hummingbird burns fuel faster, gram for gram, than nearly any other animal, so every fraction of a lick is a real cost against a real deadline. The same body that seems too fragile to survive one cold night can also cross the Gulf of Mexico in a single flight. Before the crossing, a ruby-throated hummingbird eats until it nearly doubles its weight in fat, then flies roughly five hundred miles of open water without a place to land. Two centuries of confident explanation fell to one camera and one person willing to check.

6.title: The Bird That Flies Backward
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Family Trochilidae, about 360 species, only in the Americas
Bee hummingbird of Cuba: about 2 grams, the smallest bird alive
Wings hinge almost entirely at the shoulder
Throat color is structural, not pigment
Nests are bound with spider silk so they stretch
They remember individual flowers and refill times

blocks.prompt: The Bargain: How Small a Warm Body Can Get
blocks.text: Every hummingbird alive is running an experiment in how small a warm-blooded animal can get before physics stops cooperating. The problem is surface area. A small body carries a great deal of skin relative to its volume, and skin is where heat escapes. Shrink an animal and it sheds heat faster and faster, so it must burn fuel faster and faster to stay warm. Push that far enough and the animal has to eat almost continuously simply to exist. The bee hummingbird of Cuba, the smallest bird on Earth, weighs about two grams, less than a penny. It lives at the edge of what is possible. Hummingbirds went there anyway, and they paid for the ticket three times over. They paid first in flight. A hummingbird does not flap the way a sparrow flaps. Its wing is nearly rigid and hinges almost entirely at the shoulder, sweeping forward and back through a flattened figure eight around fifty times a second. Most birds generate lift only on the downstroke. The hummingbird generates it on both halves, which is why it can hold a position in midair with the precision of a machine, and why it is the only bird that can fly backward under power for any real distance. Hovering like this burns energy faster, gram for gram, than almost any other activity in the animal kingdom. They paid second in diet. To fund the wings, a hummingbird visits hundreds or thousands of flowers a day and drinks nectar, which is essentially sugar water. That required a tool, and the tool fooled scientists for two centuries. The forked tongue looks like a pair of narrow straws, so biologists assumed it drew nectar upward by capillary action. In 2011, high-speed film showed otherwise. The tongue tips unfurl inside the nectar and then snap shut as they withdraw, trapping the liquid and hauling it back, fifteen to twenty times a second, at almost no energy cost. Nectar cannot build muscle, so the birds hunt gnats and spiders as well. And because a wasted trip is expensive, hummingbirds remember individual flowers and roughly how long each one takes to refill. They paid third in sleep. On a cold night a body this small cannot burn through until morning at full power. So the bird gives up being warm-blooded for a few hours. In torpor its temperature falls toward the temperature of the air, its heart drops from over a thousand beats a minute to around fifty, and it clings to a twig, unresponsive, closer to a cold stone than to a bird. Dawn arrives and it shivers itself back up to speed within minutes. What the bargain bought is worth the price. Hummingbirds exist only in the Americas, where roughly three hundred and sixty species have shaped themselves around flowers, and the flowers have shaped themselves right back into long tubes that a bee cannot enter but a hummingbird bill fits exactly. Their nests are walnut-sized cups bound with spider silk, which stretches as the chicks grow. Their throats are not painted with pigment at all. The color comes from stacked microscopic platelets in the feathers that cancel some wavelengths of light and reflect others, which is why a bird that looks dull brown from one angle turns molten red when it tilts its head a single degree. None of it is decoration. Every part of a hummingbird is an answer to the same question: how do you stay alive when you are this small and this expensive.
